Brazilian authorities first raised concerns with Apple about gaming apps being available to minors nearly three months ago, and Apple has now been given five business days to provide further details on its App Store safety measures. Details below.

Apple faces pressure over regulation and age verification issues

Last April, Brazilian officials separately notified Apple and Google about the alleged lack of age controls on gaming apps in their app stores.

At the time, the National Secretariat for Digital Rights (Sedigi) and the National Consumer Secretariat (Senacon) each sent letters to the two companies, inquiring whether "countless apps" were providing or facilitating minors' access to gaming platforms.

Brazil recently passed a new law called "ECA Digital," which requires app stores to restrict minors' access to gaming content. Apple subsequently introduced age verification measures for apps rated 18+ in the country.

Nonetheless, officials said their preliminary investigation found that multiple gaming apps appeared to lack proper age restrictions or federal authorisation, raising questions about the implementation of these safety measures.

Although it is difficult to know the full content of Apple's response, the relevant departments now say that Apple has answered most of their initial questions. However, the authorities are still requesting more information.

The following is excerpted from Brazil's Ministry of Justice and Public Security (published via Canaltech):

The clarifications requested include: how apps listed in Brazil verify their regulatory authorisation; the technical criteria used to distinguish simulation apps from those involving real-money wagering, including cases where apps hide or change functions after approval; and the mechanisms in place to prevent minors from accessing inappropriate content. Also requested is information on proactive monitoring procedures, risk prioritisation criteria, the average removal time after detection, and a timeline for implementing the announced remedial measures, including software

The secretariats noted that Google's response was less satisfactory and asked for further details on how it verifies authorised operators, monitors apps whose licences have been suspended or expired, measures enforcement effectiveness, and prevents minors from searching for or downloading gaming apps.

Finally, the secretariats requested that Apple and Google make their responses public, but allowed confidential information to be submitted separately with restricted access.
